title: Computational Statistical Mechanics — Lectures and labs
text: Material of the course (academic year 2026-27): lecture notes and slides, and the slides of the lab sessions, where we write, from scratch, simple C++ codes for Monte Carlo and Molecular Dynamics simulations.

title: Lab #1
text:
Today
Three parts, in two lab sessions (Part 1 in the first one, Parts 2 and 3 in the second):

Set up a development environment — compiler, terminal, editor. On Windows: WSL 2, a real Linux inside Windows.
Introduction to C++ (part I) — the object oriented paradigm: encapsulation, polymorphism, inheritance. From C to C++ with the examples N0, N1, N2 and N3.
Task: a vector class from scratch — pvector.hpp and its main in pvector.cpp: header guards, constructor and destructor, overloading of =, + and -, arguments passed by reference, this, const methods, using and constexpr.

pvector is the first brick of the simulation codes (Monte Carlo and Molecular Dynamics) we will write in the next labs: positions, velocities and forces of the particles will all be pvectors.

On Windows we do not use the native compilers (MinGW, Visual Studio): with WSL you get the same environment as on a Linux machine (and later the same packages, e.g. for the molgl visualizer).

title: Lab #1
text:
Windows: what is WSL 2
WSL = Windows Subsystem for Linux. Version 2 runs a real Linux kernel in a lightweight virtual machine managed by Windows:

you get a Linux distribution (Ubuntu by default) with its terminal, apt, g++, make, gdb, …
no dual boot, no VirtualBox: Ubuntu is an app, it starts in a few seconds;
Linux and Windows see each other’s files;
graphical Linux programs open their windows on the Windows desktop (WSLg: Windows 11, or Windows 10 from build 19044).

Requirements: Windows 11, or Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later, and hardware virtualization enabled (it usually is on recent laptops).

title: Lab #1
text:
Installing WSL 2

Open PowerShell as administrator: right click on Start → Terminal (Admin) (Windows 11) or Windows PowerShell (Admin) (Windows 10).
Run
wsl --install
It enables the required Windows features, installs WSL 2 and Ubuntu.
Restart Windows.
Open the Ubuntu app (Start menu). The first time it asks for a UNIX username and password: choose them and remember the password, it is the one sudo will ask for. While you type it nothing is shown: that is normal.
Check, from PowerShell:
wsl -l -v          # lists the distributions: Ubuntu must have VERSION 2

title: Lab #1
text:
If something goes wrong

VERSION is 1 → wsl --set-version Ubuntu 2 (use the NAME printed by wsl -l -v), and for the future wsl --set-default-version 2.
Error about virtualization (e.g. 0x80370102) → enable it in the BIOS/UEFI (Intel VT-x or AMD-V / SVM), then retry.
wsl --install only prints the help (Windows 10 not up to date) → run Windows Update first. If it still does not work, enable the two features by hand from an administrator PowerShell, restart, run wsl --update (it installs the WSL 2 kernel) and wsl --set-default-version 2, then install Ubuntu from the Microsoft Store:
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:Microsoft-Windows-Subsystem-Linux /all /norestart
dism.exe /online /enable-feature /featurename:VirtualMachinePlatform /all /norestart
Keep WSL up to date: wsl --update; general status: wsl --status.
code: command not found in Ubuntu → code comes from VS Code installed on Windows (option Add to PATH, on by default): install it first, then reopen the Ubuntu terminal (or wsl --shutdown). Do not install VS Code inside Ubuntu.

title: Lab #1
text:
Inside Ubuntu: the compiler
From the Ubuntu terminal (the same commands on a native Ubuntu/Debian machine). apt is the package manager of Ubuntu; sudo runs a command as administrator and asks for your Linux password:
sudo apt update
sudo apt install build-essential gdb unzip   # g++, gcc, make, C/C++ headers, debugger, unzip
g++ --version                           # check
On macOS the compiler comes with the Xcode command line tools:
xcode-select --install
g++ --version        # it prints "Apple clang ...": fine, g++ is an alias of clang++
On Fedora: sudo dnf install gcc-c++ make gdb.
Later in the course we will also install the libraries for molgl, the program we use to look at the configurations (freeglut, libpng): not today.

title: Lab #1

text:
WSL: where to keep your files

Work in your Linux home (~, i.e. /home/<your Linux user>), e.g. ~/csm, not on the Windows disk /mnt/c/...: compiling and running from /mnt/c is much slower.
From Linux, the Windows disk is under /mnt/c. To unpack the zips you downloaded with the browser from the course page:
mkdir -p ~/csm && cd ~/csm
unzip /mnt/c/Users/<your Windows user>/Downloads/project_classes.zip   # -> ~/csm/project
unzip /mnt/c/Users/<your Windows user>/Downloads/cpp_examples.zip     # -> ~/csm/examples
mkdir -p: no error if the folder already exists; a && b: run b only if a succeeded.
From Windows, the Linux files are in the Linux entry of File Explorer, or at \\wsl.localhost\Ubuntu\home\<your Linux user>.
Quick trick: explorer.exe . opens the current Linux folder in File Explorer.

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Object oriented (OO) paradigm
Key concepts
Encapsulation

Separate implementation from interface.
Attributes (data members) and methods (functions) can be public (→ interface) or private (→ implementation, hidden to user).
No need to know/remember internals of all objects.







Methods/functions act on objects and return objects (as an operator does) ⇓



Polymorphism — functions/methods can behave differently depending on the objects they act on: function overloading, operator overloading (e.g. + - / *), pointers.
Example: \(a + b\) (scalars) or \(\vec a + \vec b\) (vectors): operator “+” overloading.
Inheritance — in OO paradigm we have custom types called classes and we can enrich a class with more attributes and methods from base one.

title: Lab #1
text:
Example: custom types
From a non OO language (C) to an OO language (C++)

C language can be thought as a subset of C++.
In C you have objects (variables) of several different types such as char, int, float, double and operators that act on them (such as ++, --, +, *, etc.).
C++ introduces custom types (similar to struct) called “classes” and it allows operators and methods to act on them.








Note


In C you had struct which could embed attributes but not methods. Hence classes can be also thought as a generalization of “struct”.

title: Lab #1
text:
Instantiation
int, double, float ← fundamental types of C language.
If one writes
double d;   // double: type/class    d: instance of class "double", i.e. an OBJECT
Assume you have a custom type, i.e. a class, called vector which represents a vector. You can instantiate it as follows:
vector v;   // v is an instance of this class, i.e. an object
If we have
vector a, b, c;
and we “overloaded” the operators = and +, we can write
c = a + b;

title: Lab #1
section: The goal of the first labs
text:
The goal of the first labs
Similarly we can overload other operators such as ==, ++, --, *, /, *=, etc.
And this is precisely the goal of the first part of these hands-on classes, i.e.






learn how to write your own class to handle vectors and matrices for computations.

#include "./ex2_a_cpp_class.hpp"

Object created
no!
Hallo World 2

We never call constructor and destructor explicitly: the compiler does it, when the object is born and when it dies.
The class is in a header (.hpp), the main in a .cpp that #includes it: we compile only the .cpp.

text:
Arguments passed by reference
void twice_val(int x)  { x = 2*x; }   // by value: x is a COPY, the caller sees nothing
void twice_ref(int &x) { x = 2*x; }   // by reference: x is an alias of the argument

int a = 3;
twice_val(a);   // a is still 3
twice_ref(a);   // a is now 6     (no & in the call)

In a declaration int &x means reference; in an expression &a is still, as in C, the address of a.

In the class all the vector arguments are passed as const pvector&:
pvector sum(const pvector& V2) const    // the first const protects V2,
                                        // the last one the object (const method)

&: no copy of the object (for a vector of 3 doubles it is cheap, but think of a configuration of \(10^5\) particles…).
const: the method promises not to modify V2; the compiler enforces it.
Inside a method of pvector you can read the private members of another pvector: V2.v[i] is legal. Access is per class, not per object.

title: Lab #1
text:
operator= and this
The one method already implemented in the skeleton:
1pvector& operator=(const pvector& V2)   // A = B  is  A.operator=(B)
  {
    for (int i=0; i < NT; i++)
      v[i] = V2.v[i];                   // v[i] is A's, V2.v[i] is B's
2    return (*this);
  }

1

A = B is just a nicer way to write the method call A.operator=(B): A is the object the method acts on, B the argument.

2

this is a pointer: the address of the object the method has been called on (A). As in C, * applied to an address gives the object, so *this is A itself. v[i] is a shorthand for (*this).v[i].



It returns A itself by reference (pvector&): A = B = C; works as for double — it is A = (B = C) — and no copy of the vector is made.
It is not const: it changes the object.
Even without writing it, A = B works: the compiler generates a copy member by member, as for C structs. We write it to see how an operator is defined.

title: Lab #1
text:
sum(), operator+ and operator-
pvector sum(const pvector &V2) const      // C = A.sum(B)
pvector operator+(const pvector& V2) const // C = A + B   is   C = A.operator+(B)
pvector operator-(const pvector& V2) const // C = A - B
Recipe, the same for the three:

create a local vector VT;
fill it component by component, using v[i] (of A) and V2.v[i] (of B);
return VT;


They are const: A + B must change neither A nor B.
They return by value (pvector, not pvector&): VT is a local object, destroyed when the method ends. A reference to it would point to a dead object (g++ warns: reference to local variable returned).
sum() and operator+ do the same thing: the operator is just nicer to read. Once one is written, the other can call it. Same recipe as in example N3 (vecdder).

title: Lab #1
text:
get() and set()
ntype get(int i) const          // returns the i-th component
ntype set(int i, ntype val)     // sets the i-th component to val

get is const, set is not: why?
set in the skeleton returns an ntype: return val (or change it to void, as in myvec).
Components are numbered from 0 to NT-1, as in C. Nothing checks the index: get(3) reads outside the array (undefined behaviour).








Read the warnings


The empty bodies of the skeleton compile: for a method that should return a value and has no return the compiler only warns no return statement in function returning non-void [-Wreturn-type]. When the program calls it the behaviour is undefined: recent compilers stop with Illegal instruction, an older g++ may silently return a garbage value. Fill a method before testing it.

Compile, run, compare
cd ~/csm/project
g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o pvector pvector.cpp
./pvector
Expected output, if pvector() sets all components to 0 (otherwise C= and PC= show the values you chose):
C=(0,0,0)
A=(1,2,3)
B=(0.5,-1,2)
A(1)=2
A+B=(1.5,1,5)
A-B=(0.5,3,1)
A.sum(B)=(1.5,1,5)
E=(1,2,3)
PC=(0,0,0)

No warnings with -Wall: if there are, read them — they are usually a bug.
Change ntype to float: everything must still compile and run. With NT 2 the class still works, but this main does not: set(2, ...) writes outside the array, and nothing checks it.

title: Lab #1
text:
Classic pitfalls

; after the class: class pvector { ... };. Without it: error: expected ';' after class definition.
pvector P(); is not an object: it declares a function P returning a pvector. Write pvector P;.
Returning a reference to a local object in operator+: it compiles with a warning (reference to local variable 'VT' returned), then with g++ it usually crashes (Segmentation fault): undefined behaviour.
Missing const on show() or get(): then they cannot be called on a const pvector, nor on an argument const pvector& V2: passing 'const pvector' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers.
Missing return in a non-void method: only a warning, then a crash or garbage values (see get() and set()).
Header guard missing, or with the name already used by another header: error: redefinition of 'class ...' as soon as the header is included twice.

Examples N0, N1, N2, N3 compiled and run; tried to access a private member and read the error

sum(), operator+, operator- returning by value, const

Still works with ntype = float

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Example 0: compile and run
gcc -Wall -o ex0 ex0_basic_c_types.c && ./ex0
a=1 b=2 c=3
d=1.200000 e=2.300000 f=3.500000
va=(1.200000,1.300000,-1.000000
vb=(0.200000,0.100000,0.400000
vc=va+vb=(1.400000,1.400000,-0.600000)

For double we write f = d + e; for vectors vc = va + vb is not possible: every component has to be spelled out with a loop.
Printing a vector takes another loop, repeated three times (for va, vb and vc).
gcc compiles C, g++ C++: these two examples are C files.
The comment “double is a class” is an analogy: in C++ double is a fundamental type, but it behaves like a class here (objects and operators).

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Example 1: compile and run
gcc -Wall -o ex1 ex1_vec_with_funcs.c && ./ex1
va=(1.200000,1.300000,-1.000000)
vb=(0.200000,0.100000,0.400000)
vc=va+vb=(1.400000,1.400000,-0.600000)

Less repetition, but sumvec(va, vb, vc) is not vc = va + vb.
Reminder of C: an array passed to a function is not copied, the function works on the caller’s array; this is why sumvec can fill vc. char* txt is a C string (compiled with g++ it warns: in C++ "va" is a const char*).
Data (double[3]) and functions acting on them live separately: nothing tells the compiler that sumvec belongs to “vectors”.
What we want: a type vector that carries its data and its operations.
-Wall also warns that i in main is never used: warning: unused variable 'i'.

VS Code: opening the project

title: Lab #1
section: Compiling and running in VS Code
text:
Compiling and running in VS Code

The integrated terminal (Terminal → New Terminal): a normal Linux terminal (with WSL: Ubuntu’s), already in the project folder. Type the usual command, e.g. g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -o pvector pvector.cpp. In the first weeks prefer it to the ▷ button: you choose the options and read all the warnings.
The ▷ button at the top right of the editor, Run C/C++ File (C/C++ extension): with the file with main open (pvector.cpp, not pvector.hpp), choose C/C++: g++ build and debug active file (on macOS clang++). VS Code compiles the active file, runs it, and writes the recipe in .vscode/tasks.json.
The recipe lacks our options: add them at the beginning of "args" in .vscode/tasks.json:
"args": [
    "-std=c++17", "-Wall",
    ...the arguments that are already there ("-g", "${file}", ...)
],
Ctrl+Shift+B (macOS Cmd+Shift+B, Terminal → Run Build Task) compiles with the same recipe; F5 starts the debugger (we will use it later).

title: Lab #1
Lab #1
Lab #1
text:
Why the header guard

A class may be defined only once in each .cpp. If a .cpp includes the same header twice, also through another header, the class is defined twice. Example N2 without guards: vecder.hpp already includes myvec.hpp, so a main that includes both stops with error: redefinition of 'class myvec'.
The header guard prevents it: the first time _PVECTOR_ is not defined, so the file is read and the macro defined; the second time everything between #ifndef and #endif is skipped. Each header needs its own name.

Today

Introduction to C++ (part II) — protected members (example N4) and function overloading (example N5).
Lab #1: the solution — the methods of pvector you wrote last time.
Task: new constructor and operators for pvector — a constructor with an initializer_list, +=, -=, scalar product, norm(), vector times and divided by a scalar, *=, /=, == and the cross product ^.

Along the way we go back to some ideas of Lab #1 that the new methods use all the time: const methods, the pointer this and the object *this, returning by reference, const references, temporary objects.

title: Lab #2
text:
Where we left off

Inheritance (N2): class vecder: public myvec inherits all the members of myvec and adds show(). But show() cannot read v[i]: v is private in myvec, so it has to go through the public methods get() and length().
Operator overloading (N3): = and + written as methods of vecdder; v3 = v1 + v2 is v3.operator=(v1.operator+(v2)).

Today:

a third access level, between private and public: protected;
function overloading: several methods with the same name, as we did for the operators, and what happens to it in a derived class.

title: Lab #2
text:
Three access levels
Who can use a member, according to where it is declared:









member declared
methods of the class
methods of a derived class
outside (e.g. main)




private
yes
no
no


protected
yes
yes
no


public
yes
yes
yes




In a class the default is private (in a struct it is public).
protected: hidden from the users of the class, visible to who extends it.
class dercl: public basecl (public inheritance): the inherited members keep their level. The private ones are in the derived object too, but it cannot touch them.
Data private (or protected if derived classes need them), methods public. With v protected in myvec, vecder::show() (N2) could use v[i] directly.

title: Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
text:
Function overloading
Several functions (or methods) with the same name and different parameters (number or types). The compiler chooses, at compile time, from the types of the arguments:
void print(int i)          { std::cout << "int "    << i << "\n"; }
void print(double x)       { std::cout << "double " << x << "\n"; }
void print(std::string s)  { std::cout << "string " << s << "\n"; }

print(3);       // int 3
print(3.5);     // double 3.5
print("abc");   // string abc

The return type does not count: int f(int) and double f(int) together give error: ambiguating new declaration of 'double f(int)'.
In C every function needs its own name (abs, labs, fabs); in C++ one name is enough, std::abs, overloaded for int, long, double, …
We already did it with the operators: + exists for int, for double and, since Lab #1, for pvector. Today we overload the constructor of pvector and operator* (two versions).

title: Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
text:
Back to this and *this
A.norm();          // inside norm(), this == &A
D += B;            // D.operator+=(B): inside, this == &D

Every method receives an implicit argument: this, a pointer to the object it is called on. Writing v[i] inside a method means this->v[i], that is (*this).v[i]: the components of that object.
*this is the object itself (* applied to a pointer, as in C). You need it when a method must use or return the whole object:

return (*this); in operator= and today in +=, -=, *=, /=;
(*this)*(*this) in norm(): the scalar product of the object with itself.

V2.v[i] are the components of the argument, v[i] those of *this.

title: Lab #2
text:
Back to const methods
ntype norm(void) const      // const after the parameters: *this is read-only

In a const method this points to a const pvector: the method can only read the object. Assigning v[i] inside it is a compile error.
Only const methods can be called on a const object or through a const reference. A norm() without const, used on a const pvector& V: error: passing 'const pvector' as 'this' argument discards qualifiers.
So: const every method that does not change the object.








today, const
today, not const




A*B, norm(), A*s, A/s, A==B, A^B: they compute a new value
+=, -=, *=, /=: they change the object on the left

title: Lab #2
text:
Arguments by const reference
pvector& operator+=(const pvector& V2)    // vectors: by const reference
pvector& operator*=(ntype s)              // numbers: by value

const pvector&: no copy of the vector (&), and the method promises not to change it (const). Always use it for vector arguments.
A number (ntype s) is passed by value: copying a double costs nothing.
A const reference accepts temporary objects too: in A*(B+C) the argument is B+C, a vector with no name that lives only in that expression. With a non-const pvector& it does not compile: error: cannot bind non-const lvalue reference of type 'pvector&' to an rvalue of type 'pvector'.

title: Lab #2
section: Returning by value or by reference
text:
Returning by value or by reference








returns
what
when




pvector (by value)
a new vector, copied to the caller
+, -, A*s, A/s, ^: the result is a local VT


pvector& (by reference)
the object itself, no copy
=, +=, -=, *=, /=: return (*this);


ntype, bool
a number
A*B, norm(), ==




By reference only something that survives the method: *this exists before and after the call. A local VT dies at the end of the method: a reference to it points to a dead object (Lab #1).
+= returns pvector&, like operator=, so (D += B) *= 2.0; changes D twice. If it returned pvector (by value), *= 2.0 would act on a copy of D, and D would only get += B.

title: Lab #2
text:
Temporary objects: + vs +=
The operators that are not assignments (+, -, *, /, ^) must not change their operands: A + B changes neither A nor B, so the result has to go into a new object, a temporary:
D = A + B + C;   // A+B -> temporary T1;  T1+C -> temporary T2;  D = T2
                 // then T1 and T2 are destroyed
D = A;           // the same result
D += B;          // no temporary: D changes in place
D += C;

Each temporary means a constructor, a loop to fill it, a copy and a destructor. For 3 components it is nothing; with \(10^5\) particles and \(10^6\) steps it adds up.
In the simulation loops prefer the assignment operators, where you can: r += v*dt; (one temporary, v*dt) rather than r = r + v*dt; (two).

title: Lab #2
Lab #2
text:
A second constructor: initializer_list
Goal: give the components when the vector is created, with braces:
pvector A = {1.0, 2.0, 3.0};
pvector B{0.5, -1.0, 2.0};      // the same, without =

Overloading of the constructor: a class can have several constructors, with different parameters. pvector D; calls pvector(), the braces the new one (skeleton):
pvector(std::initializer_list<ntype> L)  // overloading constructor
std::initializer_list<ntype>: the list of values written between braces, all of type ntype (header <initializer_list>, already included). It cannot be changed; L.size() is the number of values.
pvector() must stay: once a class has a constructor, the compiler does not generate the void one any more, and without it pvector D; gives error: no matching function for call to 'pvector::pvector()'.

title: Lab #2
text:
Going through an initializer_list
The values of L are read with a range-based for (C++11):
for (ntype x: L)            // x takes, in turn, each value of the list
  std::cout << x << " ";    // {1.0, 2.0, 3.0} -> 1 2 3

Read it as “for each x in L”. Keep your own counter i for the component to fill.
The list may have a number of values different from NT: decide what to do. For example missing components set to 0, extra values ignored:
pvector C = {4.0};          // (4,0,0)
Never write beyond v[NT-1].

title: Lab #2
text:
Scalar product and norm()
ntype operator*(const pvector& V2) const    // s = A*B    is   s = A.operator*(B)
ntype norm(void) const                      // |A| = sqrt(A*A)

\(\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B} = \sum_{i} A_i B_i\): it returns a number (ntype), not a vector. Accumulate the sum in a local ntype initialized to 0.
norm(), \(|\mathbf{A}| = \sqrt{\mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{A}}\), must use the operator just written: (*this)*(*this) is the scalar product of the object with itself. sqrt comes from <cmath>.
Both are const.

title: Lab #2
section: Vector times and divided by a scalar
text:
Vector times and divided by a scalar
pvector operator*(ntype s) const    // A*s     a new vector
pvector operator/(ntype s) const    // A/s     a new vector

The second operator* of the class: A*B (a pvector on the right) is the scalar product, A*2.0 the vector times scalar. A*2 works too: the int 2 is converted to ntype.
2.0*A (a double on the left) does not compile: error: no match for 'operator*' (operand types are 'double' and 'pvector').
Dividing by 0 is not checked: the components become inf or nan.

title: Lab #2
text:
operator==
bool operator==(const pvector& V2) const    // if (A == B) ...

bool: true only if all the components are equal. You can return as soon as you find two different ones. std::cout prints a bool as 1 or 0.
It compares floating point numbers exactly: with E = {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}, (E*3.0)/3.0 == E is false, because 0.1*3.0 is 0.30000000000000004 (std::cout with its default 6 digits shows 0.3, which hides it).
So == is good for vectors copied from each other, not for the results of computations. Those are compared within a tolerance: (A-B).norm() < 1e-10.

title: Lab #2
text:
Cross product ^
pvector operator^(const pvector& V2) const   // C = A ^ B
\[\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B} = (A_1B_2 - A_2B_1,\; A_2B_0 - A_0B_2,\; A_0B_1 - A_1B_0)\]

It returns a new vector (local VT, by value), const.
It is defined only for NT equal to 3: otherwise print a message and stop the program with exit(1) (from <cstdlib>, already included).
Check: \(\mathbf{A}\times\mathbf{B}\) is orthogonal to \(\mathbf{A}\) and \(\mathbf{B}\), so (A^B)*A and (A^B)*B must be 0.

title: Lab #2
text:
Classic pitfalls

+= returning pvector instead of pvector&: it compiles, D += B works, but (D += B) *= 2.0 changes a copy.
Missing const on operator*, norm(), ==, ^: they cannot be used on const objects nor on const pvector& arguments (... discards qualifiers).
Argument pvector& without const: temporaries like B+C are refused (cannot bind non-const lvalue reference ...).
Sum not initialized in the scalar product: ntype sp; contains garbage, ntype sp=0;.
Removing pvector() when adding the initializer_list constructor: pvector D; no longer compiles.
Writing past v[NT-1] with a list longer than NT.
Precedence of ^: always parentheses.
== on the results of computations: use a tolerance.

title: Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
Lab #2
text:
Consequences

Inside operator+, v[i] are the components of A (*this), V2.v[i] those of B.
The const at the end of a method protects the left operand: A + B, A*B, A == B are const methods, A = B and D += B are not. The right operand is protected by the const in const pvector& V2.
The assignment operators return the left operand itself (return (*this);, type pvector&): this is why A = B = C works. The others return a new object.
A*B and A*2.0 are two different methods of A, operator*(const pvector&) and operator*(ntype): function overloading (Part 1), chosen from the type of the right operand.
2.0*A would be 2.0.operator*(A): double is not a class and has no methods, so it does not compile. In a next lab: a function outside the class (friend).
Precedence and number of operands stay those of C: the compiler applies them first, then turns A ^ B into A.operator^(B) (see the cross product).
